claims.text: The initial AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy has an intact protective oxide film formed during static exposure.
Mechanical disruption of the protective oxide film is the primary governor of accelerated tribo-corrosion degradation.
Mechanical disruption of the oxide film prevents effective repassivation.
Failure to repassivate enhances localized corrosion.
Sliding-induced mechanical stress partially removes or thins the protective oxide layer.
Oxide-film breakdown exposes fresh metal to the electrolyte and accelerates electrochemical corrosion.
Interaction between mechanical damage and corrosion produces synergistically increased overall degradation.
Increasing sliding load or speed will increase corrosion current density relative to static corrosion.
Increasing sliding load or speed will reduce passive-film impedance relative to static corrosion.
Total tribo-corrosion mass loss will exceed the sum of isolated wear loss and isolated corrosion loss.
The corrosion component of degradation will be markedly accelerated during coupled wear and corrosion.
The predicted coupling should hold for high-entropy alloys having mechanically vulnerable passive films.
Alloying or microstructural design can produce a more stable protective film.
A highly robust oxide film should make tribo-corrosion coupling negligible.
Extremely fast repassivation kinetics should make tribo-corrosion coupling negligible.
The magnitude of synergy may vary with oxide composition, microstructure, and repassivation kinetics.
Static immersion and wear in an inert medium provide isolated corrosion and wear baselines for comparison with tribo-corrosion.

The hypothesis is falsified if increasing load causes no statistically significant increase in corrosion current density and mass loss, or if passive-film impedance remains unchanged from the static baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the baselines ensure that only the wear-corrosion interaction differs and that tests use identical environmental conditions, but the wear baseline is conducted in an inert or non-corrosive medium whereas the coupled test is conducted in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. Thus the chemical environment also differs.
